I feel so dumb for not realizing my cat just wanted to be included on my desk My six year old cat has been pretty vocal most of her life this far, but recently she’s been very persistent to keep my attention. For a few weeks I figured this was due to her recent issues with a prior UTI and her discomfort with a urinary crystal (scheduled to be removed next week), so I got her a low dose prescription for gabapentin. This calmed her down a tad, but it didn’t stop her from sitting next to my chair and nipping me for attention.

Today she was meowing anytime I looked away from her after I let her into the office, so I decided to look up specifically why cats might get more demanding when you sit to work at your desk. Well, turns out this is pretty common as most of you probably know. And the most common solution I found was to make a space on the desk for the cat to feel “included.” So I shuffled some things around to fit her bed next to my work equipment on the desk.

And wouldn’t you know it, this calmed her down immediately. No more yelling in my ear. No more nips for attention. She made herself at home and continued observing me as I got to work this morning.

I’ve grown up with cats all my life. I’m 35, and I feel so silly for not even considering this prior to now. I’m always learning something new with these guys!

Edit - I’m loving all your stories and pictures of your own desk setups for the cats! It’s so fun to see how everyone has accommodated their own little supurrvisors. Thank you for sharing and teaching me a new way to keep my cats happy!

Worried about elderly cat getting out when company comes over Ok so my cat is 18 years old. Her name is Sunny. I absolutely cherish her and she adores me. I wish I could upload photos because our bond is truly something else.

My dad has family coming over next week for 3.5 days. It’s a Mormon family, so 2 adults and I believe 6-7 children between 2-10 years old. She is obviously going to feel stressed and overstimulated. My biggest concern though, is anyone- including my dad who is hosting this thing- leaving the front door open due to being distracted, and Sunny either bolting outside (she has obvious cognitive decline, developing cataracts, and can’t hear very well at all. I have to be careful greeting her because she gets easily startled because she can’t hear me approaching) where she could get lost and NOT FIND HER WAY BACK HOME, or people being oblivious, or kids being kids, and shutting her outside by mistake or ignorance and forgetfulness or mindlessness of the boundaries I am going to set as far as leaving the front door open. If she gets out and strays from the house, she WILL NOT BE ABLE TO FIND HER WAY BACK HOME. it’s every animal owners worst fear, right? Never knowing or having any idea how this thing you deeply love is doing. If it’s ok. Where it is.

So basically, big risk with so many kids coming over.
My dad is in his 60s, but has the emotional intelligence of a carrot, or any other vegetable really. He is basically like a young teenager when it comes to confrontation and he does not take many of the safeguards seriously when it comes to Sunny. Despite me showing studies and evidence about the risks and limitations of a super elderly cat, he doesn’t agree, and you can tell he doesn’t buy some things I say AT ALL. how he felt about something beforehand is all the evidence he needs to feel completely justified and valid about things. He is right because he feels he is right. I don’t trust him to be careful with the front door or the kids not overwhelming her at all. He thinks I am being WAY TOO overprotective, despite me referencing and trying to show the studies. Acute stress can absolutely cause physical damage to an 18 year old cat ( such as a bunch of kids pestering her for 3 days). He doesn’t buy that. I showed him evidence and he just rolls his eyes and he says “ok” sarcastically. In his mind I’m being overboard protective. Evidence doesn’t matter. He doesn’t believe the cat could be a flight risk with stress being inside and the door being left open. I don’t think he’s been receptive to anything anyone has ever said except his mom or religious figures.

WHAT CAN I DO TO SAFEGUARD THE CAT while I am at work??! I am thinking of buying one of those dog gates they use to keep dogs out of certain rooms. There is the front door, a small porch, and then an entry to the small stairs leading off the porch. I can put the gate there at the top of the stairs. She is too old to easily jump on top of the porch fence and over very easily or quickly. It’s at least a buffer. I am also thinking about moving the litter box from the garage to my room as well so she doesn’t have to walk through the madness of 6-7 small children to do her business.

Is there anything else I can do to safeguard Sunny for the 9-13 hours I am at work for those few days?! I’m genuinely scared and spiraling about this. Sitting down and trying to have a rational conversation about my concerns with my dad (who will be the only one home all day for this as he is retired) will be about as productive as trying to set boundaries with an angry 13 year old teenager. I’m not exaggerating the dude needs therapy.

TL/DR: my kitty is 18 years old and cannot navigate or survive outside anymore. A bunch of family the cat has never met, between the ages of 2-10, are coming over for a few days during my work week. I can’t trust my dad to be as careful as believe I need him to be to ensure the front door isn’t left open by anyone and the kids don’t overstimulate her. What can I do to safeguard the kitty’s safety while me and my mom are both at work?

Always consult with a medical professional when you suspect something may be going on :) in my case I have had these symptoms for years and never explored sleep apnea as a diagnosis and wouldn’t have thought to do so until now, after noticing this pattern thanks to Bast. Looking for Advice on My Cat’s Behavioral Issues—At a Breaking Point Hi everyone,

I have a female cat named Peppa, who has been with me for eight years. I adopted her when she was around 2–3 months old, and even then, I could tell something was different about her. She has always exhibited unusual behaviors that make daily care incredibly challenging.

Peppa struggles with eating—she picks at her dry food like the chicken from Moana, barely consuming enough. She avoids jumping unless she has just pooped, and even then, if she gets onto the bed or furniture, she won’t come down by herself. She seems afraid of heights.

One of the biggest difficulties is her litter box usage. She rarely goes on her own and requires us to manually place her in the box 2–3 times per day. When she needs to pee or poop, she starts walking in circles until she can no longer hold it, relieving herself wherever she happens to be.

I’ve always done my best to give Peppa a good life. But after welcoming my first daughter, things have become overwhelming. Emotionally, it’s draining. Financially, it’s unsustainable.

Whenever we leave the house for more than eight hours, I have to hire a pet sitter to come multiple times a day just to put Peppa in the litter box and feed her wet food (she won’t eat dry food). Every vacation is a nightmare—she leaves a mess, and I come home to ruined furniture and carpets. I’ve already had to evacuate my master bedroom because she has urinated and defecated on my bed and every spot in the room. Now, I have to replace the carpet, which is another major expense that I can’t currently afford.

Peppa sees the vet regularly. Every test comes back normal except for a few UTIs in the past. My vet believes her issues are behavioral and recommended seeing a neurologist—but warned that it would be expensive, and there might not be a fix.

Her condition has only worsened over time. I can’t keep her in the living room anymore because she has already ruined multiple pieces of furniture. And now that I have a baby, it’s simply not sanitary to have them together.

The vet has suggested euthanasia. I've never had to make this kind of decision for a pet before. I’m completely torn. I don’t know what the right thing to do is, but this situation is impacting my relationship, my home life, and my mental well-being. I used to have the bandwidth to dedicate myself to her needs, but I just don’t anymore.

I’m exhausted. I feel guilty. And I don’t know what to do.

Has anyone been through something similar? Are there any solutions I haven’t tried? I would really appreciate any advice or insight you can offer.

Thank you.

text:
Common Health Problems Of Cats If you are new to owning a cat, you may be surprised to find that health problems are a common thing. No matter what breed of cat you own, health problems are to be expected. Some can be hereditary, while others can be easily avoided.

Worms Regardless of the breed of cat, worms are a very common and recurring problem. Tapeworms, roundworms and hookworms are among the most common that infect cats. Cats that have weight gain problems, flea problems, or if you find white spots in his stool, you should ask your veterinarian to test him for worms. Although they can be treated with medication, worms can prove fatal if left untreated.

Hair balls Hairballs are the most common health problem for cats. All cats groom themselves daily, normally swallowing the loose hairs that come from their coats. Occasionally, these loose hairs will gather in a ball and lodge in the digestive tract instead of passing through your cat's stool. When your cat starts coughing and hacking, it normally spits out a hairball. Although it can be rather disgusting in the end, most cats can dislodge the hairballs without any problems.

In rare cases, a hairball can pass through the intestine of a cat, creating a blockage. Blockages are very serious problems and can be life-threatening if left untreated. If your cat becomes constipated, does not eat properly, or has a very dull coat, it could have a blockage. If you notice any of these symptoms, you should immediately take him to the veterinarian. You can prevent hairballs and blockages by brushing your cat 2 or 3 times a week to remove loose hair. You can also give him food designed to control the hairballs.

Urinary tract infection Urinary tract infection is also a common health problem in cats. Urinary tract infection is more common in male cats that have not been sterilized, although females can also suffer from this problem. When a cat suddenly stops going to its litter box, this problem is normally the cause. Another symptom is when the cat's urine begins to smell very strongly. If you suspect that your cat has a urinary tract infection, you should take it to the vet. Your veterinarian can treat the problem with medication and make recommendations to help avoid this problem in the future.

Feline leukemia In the past, feline leukemia was the biggest cause of death in cats. These days however, there are vaccines available that can treat the disease. To treat the disease, your cat will need to receive the vaccine before being exposed. Even if death does not occur immediately, cats exposed to feline leukemia normally have a long lifespan. If you know that your cat has feline leukemia, you should never allow other cats around him, as the virus is very contagious.

To protect your cat, you should always make sure to take her to the vet for her regular checkups. If you keep him informed of his vaccinations, he should lead a healthy and productive life. Although some health problems can be prevented, most of them can. You can also keep your cat indoors, which will protect it from the majority of health problems. If your cat is an outdoor cat, regular visits to the veterinarian will keep it healthy. As long as you take your cat to the vet and keep it healthy, it will be your companion for years to come.
